claims.text: The starting FeNiCoCrAl-based protective coating contains both FCC and BCC regions.
The starting coating has randomly distributed, poorly controlled FCC/BCC interfaces with high lattice misfit.
Changing spray-deposition parameters can alter the phase constitution, oxidation, and defect structure of FeNiCoCrAl-family coatings.
Post-deposition annealing can be used to tailor the coating microstructure at about 800 °C.
Controlled spraying and annealing can produce coherent FCC/BCC interfaces with reduced or negative lattice misfit.
Reduced or moderately negative interphase lattice misfit promotes interface coherency and generates interfacial elastic strain.
The optimized interfacial strain fields impede dislocation climb and reduce atomic diffusion.
Interface-mediated dislocation locking delays shear-band formation and promotes more uniform deformation.
Optimized coatings will have a 20–30% lower creep strain rate than baseline coatings under identical loading.
Optimized coatings will show delayed shear-band initiation and a more uniform strain distribution than baseline coatings.
Coatings with higher lattice misfit will exhibit higher creep rates than coatings with optimized misfit.
Baseline coatings will initiate localized shear deformation earlier than optimized coatings.
The proposed creep-resistance benefit operates at 800 °C under sustained stresses of 300–600 MPa.
At sufficiently high stress or temperature, the creep mechanism can change and the interface-derived benefit can diminish.
Loss of FCC/BCC interface coherency is the reason for diminished creep resistance above the operating boundary.
Spray-induced oxidation, phase-fraction changes, and porosity can confound attribution of creep behavior to lattice misfit alone.
Failure of the interface-optimized group to show statistically significant improvement over a controlled baseline would falsify the proposed causal role of reduced FCC/BCC misfit.
